column4: Hmm. A flask of oil, such as that used by woodworkers or leatherworkers to finish their handiwork. But I do not recognize the odor, nor the stag device inscribed on the flask. All I can say is that it is very old. - Muzah-Tei
column5: I know the stag symbol. It is fairly commonplace in the Reach. It represents one of the aspects of Hircine, the Great Stag. This oil is sacred to Hircine, likely used to anoint and consecrate a relic of great value. - Verita Numida
column6: Oh! That would be Uricanbeg. Those who hear the drumbeat of his hooves are doomed to run with the herd. To be chased and unmade, as the Reachfolk say. A warrior wearing the mask imbued by this oil would drive his enemies from him in terror. - Amalien

column4: Teeth? No, fangs. The scrimshaw is definitely Reachfolk work. I believe the markings represent a chant to Hircine in his aspect as Alrabeg, the Hunter: The five are all, the five are one. Five are true and death-in-the-woods. - Verita Numida
column5: Five is a number that comes up with Hircine. These fangs represent the Spear of Bitter Mercy, also called Spear with Five Points. They would have been fixed in a war-mask belonging to a great chief of the Ket Keptu. - Ugron gro-Thumog
column6: Ah, of course! The Ket Keptu were hunters and warrior-smiths, a people devoted to the Lord of the Hunt. To carry the Spear of Bitter Mercy was a high honor for their great champions. Whoever wore this war-mask was indeed favored by Hircine! - Reginus Buca

column4: Is this a scarf? No, it's a headwrap made from some sort of felt. I believe it is part of a ceremonial Reachfolk mask. A shaman or chief would wear this beneath the mask itself. Curious. The cloth part of a mask is usually the first part to rot away. - Verita Numida
column5: It is not felt made from wool, but the fur of a fox. A Reachfolk mask incorporating fox-fur certainly suggests Hircine worship. A fox is one of the Huntsman's aspects. - Muzah-Tei
column6: Reachfolk know that aspect of Hircine as Gulibeg, the Quick Fox. He seeks to confound mortal hunters and run them in circles until they are so confused they follow him over a cliff or into a mire. - Reginus Buca

column4: Now this is interesting. A carved wooden face-mask in the shape of a snarling beast's snout. I saw similar relics when I visited the Shrine of the Hunt-Father in Markarth. The shaman there explained that it represented an aspect of Hircine. - Verita Numida
column5: That's Hrokkibeg, the Mighty Bear. Reachfolk believe he comes to our world seeking solitude and a renewal of his spirit, but beware. If you disturb his rest, he will tear you asunder! - Amalien
column6: Ancient Nedic heroes of the Ket Keptu often wore bear emblems or totems. I think the war-mask this snout was a part of must have belonged to an important war-chief or hunt-leader. A champion of Hircine. - Ugron gro-Thumog

column4: A leather cowl of Reachfolk workmanship. Reach shamans still wear such coverings as part of various beast-themed headdresses or warmasks, but I suspect this is quite old. I do not recognize the leather. - Ugron gro-Thumog
column5: That's because this is no ordinary leather. It's made of hide blessed for shape-changing. I imagine it belonged to a powerful Reachfolk shaman, a follower of Hircine. He is the Father of Manbeasts, after all. - Amalien
column6: Uraccanach the Witchman described the Manbeast as one of the five aspects of Hircine that Reachfolk worship. They call this aspect Storihbeg. He comes to the wild places of Nirn to hunt with his children, the Skinshifters. - Reginus Buca
